figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Raven As An Open Multi-Agent Ecosystem. (a) Built-in and third-party agents expose executable model–harness pairs through execution adapters. The Host Agent uses registry capabilities to compose and assign tasks, while the runtime validates the plan, schedules ready nodes, and records artifacts for handoff and reuse. (b) An illustrative FPS game project combines gameplay development and visual design before integration, testing, and operation. Nodes denote agent calls, and directed edges denote artifact dependencies coordinated by Raven. Persistent context, reusable skills, and harness evolution support adaptation across tasks.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Harness composition. (a) A model and its harness form a callable execution unit. (b) A host assigns and coordinates these units. figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Graph planning and admission. (a) The host context carries only a summary of the orchestration guide. The host loads the full guide when a request needs several agents and delegates directly otherwise. A rejected graph returns its first error with a pointer back to the guide. In the admitted graph, R1 and R2 are the running example’s research nodes $v_{\mathrm{alg}}$ and $v_{\mathrm{bench}}$, C is $v_{\mathrm{code}}$, and D is $v_{\mathrm{design}}$. (b) A submission is a flat node list with graph-level flags. Five groups of checks run in order before any worker is dispatched (Table 1).

citing_sentences: Section 3.1 describes the first two stages (Figure 4).
Raven therefore discloses its orchestration guidance in stages (Figure 4a).
The runtime admits a graph only after five groups of checks (Figure 4b and Table 1).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Node execution and host intervention. (a) A node runs once all predecessors have completed and settled. Returned output and raised errors both reach the judge. A failed verdict suspends the node for a host decision when continuations remain. Memory recording runs asynchronously and does not delay successors. (b) Top: the judge reads the rendered prompt, output, and transcript tail, and a negative verdict becomes an exception report for the host. Bottom: a worker’s clarification request is answered from the host’s conversation and memory when possible, and otherwise reaches the user.
figures.headline: A failed verdict suspends a node for host decision, while worker clarification requests are answered from memory when possible.
citing_sentences: Section 3.2 describes the next two (Figure 5), and Section 3.3 describes the artifact and memory flow that supports reuse (Figure 6).
Once a graph is admitted, each node moves through a small set of runtime states (Figure 5a).
An independent model call therefore judges each finished node (Figure 5b).

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Artifact and memory flow. (a) A node’s prompt is rendered from its template, upstream outputs, upstream memory paths, and files. The runtime writes the prompt, output, and transcript to disk, and a memory record follows asynchronously. Successors read these files on demand. (b) The host receives a run report with paths and terminal outputs. Completed nodes enter a session-wide registry, so a later graph can reference their outputs and a single delegation can continue their instance. In (b), R3 and R4 are research nodes of a follow-up graph whose slide-deck node P references earlier outputs, and the spawn call continues the coding instance C.
figures.headline: Successor nodes read upstream outputs from files on demand, and completed nodes stay reusable in a session-wide registry.
citing_sentences: Section 3.2 describes the next two (Figure 5), and Section 3.3 describes the artifact and memory flow that supports reuse (Figure 6).
When a run finishes, the host receives a compact report that summarizes intermediate outcomes (Figure 6b).
Each handoff uses a recorded file containing the producer’s output (Figure 6a).

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Shared group memory. (a) The host mediates access to owner-partitioned EverOS libraries. It retrieves experience before planning, deposits round summaries and outcomes in its shared library, and writes agent assessments to the corresponding agent libraries. Dispatch prefetch combines shared experience with recent assessments from a provenance ledger, with respective caps $k_{\rm group}$ and $k_{\rm verdict}$. Personal user memory is excluded, while workers retain their ordinary memory access. Offset outlines indicate one library and worker per mapped agent. (b) Assessment has two phases: a close verdict after execution and a feedback verdict on the next user turn. Attribution is extracted from the host’s reply and omitted from the user-visible response and session log.
figures.headline: The host mediates owner-partitioned memory libraries, combining shared experience with recent assessments at dispatch.
citing_sentences: To incorporate this broader feedback, shared group memory converts these observations into assessments that inform future orchestration and worker invocations (Figures 7 and 3.4).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Harness self-evolution. (a) Four strategy interfaces expose decisions around a frozen model. The shared execution shell handles dispatch and accounting. (b) The best training-evaluated harness supplies failure traces for diagnosis and candidate generation. The bank stores one complete harness per edit-category/pathology cell. P/K/R/C denote prompt, knowledge, runtime, and configuration edits. The first $N_{\rm keep}$ candidates passing validity, activation, and paired-gain screening receive full-training evaluation before cell competition, where $N_{\rm keep}$ is the per-round survivor cap. The final training-selected harness is frozen before held-out testing.
figures.headline: Four strategy interfaces expose decisions around a frozen model, and the gene bank keeps one harness per edit cell.
citing_sentences: Figure 8 connects the editable policy to the search procedure.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Memory formation and consolidation in EverOS. (a) Semantic boundaries group dialogue and tool interactions into a source segment $\mathsf{seg}_{i}$. Its episode $\mathsf{ep}_{i}$ anchors atomic facts. The dashed branch derives optional foresight with validity interval $[t_{p,0},t_{p,1}]$. (b) Across interaction history $\mathsf{Hist}$, episodes, shown as points, form MemScenes around centroids marked by crosses. These scenes select evidence for profile updates. The agent track consolidates execution cases $c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}$ into reusable procedures, depicted by a small dependency graph. The diagram shows representation and data dependencies. Persistence and indexing proceed separately.
figures.headline: Memory formation groups dialogue into source segments that yield episodes, facts, and scenes, which then support profile updates.
citing_sentences: Figure 9 summarizes the formation and consolidation process, while Figure 10 shows the retrieval path used for Raven’s user memory.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Raven’s user-memory retrieval through EverOS hybrid. (a) BM25 and dense search retrieve episodes. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) determines their expansion order. A separate calibrated score ranks them for final selection. (b) The query scores facts belonging to each expanded episode. Episodes and facts compete within a bounded candidate set. A selected fact is returned under its parent episode, which restores its context. The positive integer $k_{\rm mem}$ is the backend candidate-set cap.
figures.headline: User-memory retrieval combines lexical and dense search over episodes, then returns selected facts under their parent episodes.
citing_sentences: Figure 9 summarizes the formation and consolidation process, while Figure 10 shows the retrieval path used for Raven’s user memory.
Retrieval remains within the selected user partition, following the search and response flow in Figure 10.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Skill selection and experience-driven updates. (a) Ranked source hits are grouped by name and fused before body retrieval, runtime policy checks, and LLM selection. The normal gate selects a bounded list, while a gate failure uses a separate ranked fallback. Resource resolution is attempted after selection. (b) A case enters an intent cluster and conditions skill operations together with existing skills and a bounded set of supporting cases. Persisted revisions become candidates for later EverOS retrieval after indexing. The positive integer $k_{\rm pool}$ is the fused skill-pool cap. Numeric labels show the implementation defaults in Section B.3.
figures.headline: Source hits are fused by name before an LLM gate selects skills, and execution cases condition later skill operations.
citing_sentences: Figure 11 shows how corpus admission, task-specific selection, and experience-driven revision connect.

abstract: As large language models advance, AI agents are moving beyond isolated, domain-specific tasks toward long-horizon, cross-domain workflows. This transition exposes two challenges: increasing harness complexity makes manual design difficult to scale, while tighter coupling to specific domains limits the generality of a single harness. The central question thus shifts from how to engineer a stronger harness for one domain to how to autonomously construct specialized harnesses, improve them through experience, and orchestrate them across domains. We introduce Raven, The Harness of Harnesses, an open-source multi-agent ecosystem that automatically constructs and evolves modular harnesses for specific models and domains, treating each executable model–harness pair as a composable unit of intelligence. To support an All-Domain Collaboration Network, its Host Agent decomposes goals, matches subtasks to specialized agents, coordinates execution dependencies, and integrates results, while a host archive and EverOS preserve experience across tasks and Skill Forge makes that experience available as reusable procedures. Our theory establishes sufficient conditions for such composition to expand reliable task coverage beyond that of the available individual agents under a shared resource budget. On complex and long-horizon tasks, Raven significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art agent systems, pushing the frontier of composable agentic intelligence.

sections.body: The paper argues that agent results depend on the harness around a model, and that manual harness design and single-domain harnesses limit scale and generality. Raven is an open-source ecosystem that treats each executable model–harness pair as a composable unit. Its Host Agent matches subtasks to registered agents, represents dependencies as a directed acyclic graph, and integrates their results. The roster includes four native specialists and third-party agents such as Claude Code and Codex, connected through execution adapters. Planning is evaluated on the Multi-Agent Orchestration Benchmark, where Raven leads on all four graph metrics under both backbones.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Raven composes model–harness agents through a host that plans, dispatches, and integrates work across domains.

sections.body: The theory defines a harnessed agent as a model with its tool interfaces, context and memory mechanisms, skills, and control rules. Capability is task-relative: a task counts as reliably covered when a system succeeds with probability at least $1-\delta$ within a cost budget $B$. Sufficient conditions on contracts, handoffs, and bounded planning and execution errors then yield reliable coverage of a task family under a shared budget. The section states that these are sufficient conditions, that they do not show strict improvement over every single agent, and that measured average success rates alone do not establish the conditional premises. A finite-query limit shows that black-box search with fewer queries than positions cannot guarantee finding every target.
sections.heading: Theory
sections.headline: Under a shared budget, sufficient conditions let composed agents reliably cover tasks that individual agents cannot reliably solve alone.

sections.body: Raven's collaboration layer composes heterogeneous harnesses rather than configuring roles within one framework. The Host Agent submits a typed dependency graph, and the runtime checks format, graph structure, capability, agent status, environment, and dispatch budget before any worker starts. Workers run as their dependencies settle, each result is judged, and a run report returns file locations to the host. Completed nodes are reused by reference in later graphs. Attribution verdicts are written to memory after a round and can be revised on the next user turn. The section states that verdicts are observational judgments that may be incorrect, and that group memory is disabled by default and not evaluated.
sections.heading: Multi-Agent Collaboration
sections.headline: A typed dependency graph is validated before dispatch, and every handoff passes through a recorded artifact.

sections.body: Harness self-evolution keeps the model frozen and edits a harness made of Memory, Planning, Capability, and Action strategy interfaces. A Task Agent runs tasks, an Evolver Agent proposes edits within allowed locations, and a fixed Evaluator scores them. Failure diagnosis yields candidate harnesses that are screened on training tasks with a paired t-style statistic and a fixed cutoff of $1.96$ before full-training evaluation. The archive keeps one harness per edit-category and pathology cell. The selected harness is frozen and then compared with the initial harness on held-out tasks. The section states two limits: repeated adaptive screening gives no family-wise significance guarantee, and the returned harness is not guaranteed to be globally optimal.
sections.heading: Agent Harness Self-Evolution
sections.headline: Harness evolution edits a frozen model's strategy interfaces and keeps candidates only after paired screening.

sections.body: EverOS organizes memory into episodes, atomic facts, foresight with validity intervals, and scenes formed by online clustering of episode embeddings. Raven's user recall combines hybrid episode retrieval with competition among facts, returns each selected fact under its parent episode, and adds the user's profile as a result with an adapter-assigned score of $1.0$. The host adds a Markdown archive, selecting two profile sections by lexical overlap and all Notes sections, and marks recalled content as untrusted context. Records persist as Markdown and can rebuild the search index. The section states that the $1.0$ score is a placement convention, not a relevance estimate, and that agent cases and skills stay out of the user memory segment.
sections.heading: Memory System
sections.headline: EverOS memory consolidates episodes into scenes and profiles, and Raven recalls them through hybrid retrieval.

sections.body: Skill Forge builds on SkillCorpus, whose reference release contains 96,401 active skills after deduplication, judging, and admission. Semantic deduplication merges pairs with cosine similarity above $0.995$ and sends pairs in $(0.90,0.995]$ to LLM adjudication. Release admission rejects records with hard flags such as `prompt_injection` or a safety score below 0.3. Raven's online router queries local, memory-derived, and SkillHub sources, fuses hits by name within a pool cap of `k_pool`, and passes bounded bodies to a selection gate. Execution cases are clustered by task intent and converted into add or update operations, which must meet minimum length rules. The section states that a structurally accepted update or a high confidence does not establish an improvement in task performance.
sections.heading: Skill Forge
sections.headline: Skill Forge fuses skills from three sources, selects them through a gate, and revises skills from execution cases.

sections.body: The orchestration benchmark contains 140 requests, each with a reference graph over four specialist domains, and includes all 11 domain subsets with at least two domains. Graph agreement is scored with node and transitive-reduction edge F1, and the section reports Raven ranking first on all four metrics under both backbones. For skills, SkillsBench gains are 6.5 and 13.4 points for Raven with Qwen3.5-27B and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, against 4.2 and 5.8 points for OpenClaw. The section states limits: reference graphs are authored with Claude Opus 5 and reviewed by experts, lexical filtering cannot rule out paraphrased planning cues, and individual-cell GDPval gains of 1.2 to 1.9 points are not statistically distinguishable from zero.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: Raven ranks first on all four graph metrics under both backbones, with Exact Match gains of 10.4 and 10.5 percentage points.

sections.body: Related work covers multi-agent frameworks such as AutoGen and MetaGPT, executable graph systems, harness optimization, agent memory systems, and skill libraries. The section contrasts conversation-oriented collaboration, which lacks a typed graph that can be validated before execution, with Raven's explicit artifact contracts at the orchestration boundary. For harness evolution it contrasts prompt-only and workflow optimization with a fixed edit vocabulary and gated screening. For memory and skills it separates memory records from graph edges and skill selection from tool permission. The section notes open problems, including verifying open-ended language-model execution and attributing a measured score to a specific edit.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work spans orchestration, harness evolution, agent memory, and skills, which Raven combines with explicit boundaries.

sections.body: The conclusion restates Raven as an ecosystem that composes model–harness pairs through a host with explicit task dependencies, with harness evolution, persistent memory, and Skill Forge supporting reuse. It summarizes the theory's sufficient conditions and the main results: planning gains of 10.4 and 10.5 percentage points over the strongest baseline, and skill gains larger than OpenClaw's on two of three benchmarks. Future work proposes a Raven instance per device, agent-to-agent communication among instances, connected memory, and synchronized execution progress. The stated evaluation targets are task success, continuity of user experience, and coordination cost. These networked capabilities are proposed directions, not reported results.
sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
sections.headline: Raven's conclusion summarizes planning and skill results and proposes a multi-device network as future work.

sections.body: The appendix provides a notation table, operation records and serial execution semantics, and a ledger extension argument. It gives the finite-query coverage limit with its proof and the workflow reliability argument from local experiments. It states that concurrent execution requires an additional trace-preservation premise. The remaining sections describe the experiment protocols: the scientific tasks with specified budgets and manual rubrics, skill-retrieval grading and accounting, the Claude Opus 4.7 frontier check, the single-run ablation, and the standalone retrieval evaluation. The appendix closes with the author list.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix contains notation, execution semantics, the finite-query limit, and details of benchmark, grading, and ablation protocols.
